This pack is CORPUS-ONLY and does not touch packages/snap-rules or the oracle fixture. Delaware is built as part of a five-agent parallel batch (RI, MT, DE, SD, ND) built concurrently by separate agents. Drafted from direct live fetches of dhss.delaware.gov and regulations.delaware.gov (both accessible with no WAF barrier), the regulations.delaware.gov API PDF endpoint for the full DSSM 9000 manual, the archived DSSM 2000 manual PDF, and the Delaware Register of Regulations' own repeal order for DSSM 2027 — cross-checked for internal staleness within Delaware's own regulatory text (DSSM lagging DHSS's live consumer pages in several specific, confirmed places).
_provenance.source_fact_check: direct fetch of dhss.delaware.gov's live SNAP and SNAP Alert consumer pages, cross-referenced against a direct fetch of the full 114-page DSSM 9000 Food Stamp Program manual (regulations.delaware.gov API PDF endpoint) and the archived DSSM 2000 Case Processing Procedures manual, checked specifically for staleness: DSSM 9045's resource-limit text, DSSM 9018.2/9018.3's ABAWD age-exemption text, and DSSM 9013.2's drug-felony cross-reference were each caught as lagging currently-operative Delaware policy and are flagged explicitly rather than relied on at face value; findings and gaps recorded in PROVENANCE.md
_provenance.access_note: dhss.delaware.gov and regulations.delaware.gov both returned clean HTTP 200 to every direct curl attempt this pack made — no WAF/bot-detection wall of the kind this roster's New Hampshire and Maine packs encountered. regulations.delaware.gov's human-facing AdminCode pages are a client-side JavaScript SPA with no server-rendered content; this pack located and used the underlying /api/AdminCode/titleNN/NNNN/<uuid> PDF endpoints instead (found via WebSearch results, not by reverse-engineering the SPA). usda.gov (hosting the FY26 SUA methodology memo, a separate host from fns.usda.gov) returned a clean HTTP 403 to direct curl; resolved via the r.jina.ai reader proxy, though the memo itself turned out to be methodology-only (no Delaware-specific dollar table), leaving Delaware's FY2026 SUA dollar figures a disclosed gap rather than a fabricated number.

supplements.citation: Delaware DHSS SNAP consumer page (dhss.delaware.gov); Delaware ASSIST portal (assist.dhss.delaware.gov); DSSM 9000 (Food Stamp Program)
supplements.heading: Delaware's public brand is plain "SNAP," but its own regulatory text still carries two older program names side by side — "Food Stamp Program" and "Food Supplement Program (FSP)"
supplements.text: Delaware DHSS's live consumer-facing materials use only the generic federal name "SNAP" (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) — this pack found no distinctive Delaware-specific program nickname the way California has "CalFresh" or Washington has "Basic Food." But Delaware's own regulatory text is a genuine naming time-capsule: DSSM chapter 9000 is still titled "9000 Food Stamp Program" and its Statement of Purpose still refers to "the Food Stamp Act of 1977" — the pre-2008 federal name, never updated in that specific heading even though Congress renamed the federal program SNAP in the 2008 Farm Bill. Elsewhere in the SAME manual, later-amended sections (e.g., DSSM 9018.2, on ABAWD work requirements) instead use "Food Supplement Program (FSP)" — a second, different internal name. This pack reads this as an honest artifact of a regulatory manual amended section-by-section over decades rather than a substantive policy difference, but flags it explicitly since an applicant searching Delaware's own official rules text for "SNAP" by name will not find that exact phrase in the oldest, unamended sections. Delaware's current self-service application portal is Delaware ASSIST (assist.dhss.delaware.gov), administered by DHSS's Division of Social Services (DSS). Applicants can also apply in person at any Delaware State Service Center. The Food Bank of Delaware operates SNAP Outreach assistance. Delaware's SNAP program is administered directly and centrally by DHSS's DSS — a state-administered program with no county-level policy authority, structurally similar to this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, North Carolina, Ohio, New Jersey, Tennessee, Indiana, Missouri, Maryland, Colorado, South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Utah, Iowa, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, New Mexico, and New Hampshire packs, and distinct from county-administered states like CA, NY, MN, WI, and VA.

supplements.citation: Delaware DHSS SNAP consumer page (Food Benefit Income Eligibility Limits table, published for 10/1/2025-9/30/2026); DSSM 9042 (Categorically Eligible Households); DSSM 9045 (Maximum Allowable Resources)
supplements.heading: STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING: Delaware's SNAP categorical-eligibility gate is 200% FPL gross income, triggered by a TANF-funded pregnancy-prevention-information service embedded directly in the application form — households that clear it face NO resource test; households that don't still face a real, and DSSM-text-STALE, $2,000/$3,000 limit
supplements.text: Delaware DHSS's own current Food Benefit Income Eligibility Limits table (published for October 1, 2025 - September 30, 2026) lists four income columns by household size: the 200% FPL gross-income limit that most households must meet ($2,610 for household size 1, $5,360 for size 4), a narrower 165% FPL 'Elderly / Disabled Separate Household' gross-income test ($2,152 for size 1), the underlying 130% FPL standard gross-income limit ($1,696 for size 1), and the 100% FPL net-income limit that applies to all households ($1,305 for size 1). Per DSSM 9042, any household with gross income at or below 200% FPL is CATEGORICALLY ELIGIBLE for SNAP in Delaware — not because Delaware runs a generic 'BBCE' program the way most secondary sources describe it, but through a specific, distinctive state mechanism this pack read directly from DSSM 9042's own text: Delaware uses TANF funds to provide non-cash pregnancy-prevention information (satisfying the 3rd statutory purpose of the federal TANF program), and an authorization for this information is embedded directly in the Delaware SNAP application itself. Per DSSM 9045, categorically eligible households 'do not have to meet the resource limits or definitions' at all — meaning the large majority of Delaware SNAP households, cleared via the 200% FPL gate, face no asset test whatsoever, consistent with several secondary sources' flat 'no asset limit in Delaware' claim. But this pack flags that claim as imprecise rather than universally true, the same way this roster's New Hampshire pack flagged its own three-track structure: a household that is NOT categorically eligible (excluded per DSSM 9042.2/9042.3, e.g. for an ineligible-alien member, student-provision ineligibility, fleeing-felon/probation-violator status, non-exempt institutionalization, or work-requirement noncompliance) DOES face a real, enforced resource limit under DSSM 9045's own text — and this pack found that text itself to be a genuine data-freshness problem: DSSM 9045 literally states $2,000 for most households and $3,000 for households with an elderly (60+) or disabled member, figures this pack traced to at least a 2009-era baseline with no visible newer amendment, while the current federal FY2026 COLA-adjusted resource-limit floor that 7 CFR 273.8(a) sets nationally is $3,000/$4,500. This pack could not confirm whether Delaware's own DSSM text is simply unamended paperwork lag (with the operative, federally-conforming figure actually being $3,000/$4,500 in practice) or a genuine, if unusual, state-specific sub-federal figure — and explicitly declines to guess, flagging this precisely in freshness.json rather than picking one number with false confidence.

supplements.citation: DSSM 2027 (Repealed, per 21 DE Reg. 722, effective 3/11/2018); DSSM 9042.2 (Categorically Eligible Households exclusion list, no drug-felony category); House Bill No. 11 (2017); 31 Del. C. §524
supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP FINDING (primary-source, reached by chasing a specific repealed citation rather than accepting a secondary-source paraphrase): Delaware FULLY repealed its drug-felony SNAP/Cash Assistance restriction in 2018 — several secondary sources describing a 'modified' ban are out of date
supplements.text: 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2) sets a federal default: anyone convicted of a state or federal felony for possessing, using, or distributing a controlled substance is permanently ineligible for SNAP unless a state opts out or modifies the ban under § 862a(d)(1). This pack found several secondary sources describing Delaware as having a 'modified' drug-felony ban conditioned on sentence compliance or treatment-program participation — language this pack traced back to DSSM 2027's OWN PRE-2018 text (a drug-felony disqualification did exist in Delaware's regulations at one point). But this pack fetched Delaware's own current DSSM 2000-series text directly and found DSSM 2027 marked plainly '[Repealed - See 21 DE Reg. 722 (03/01/18)]' — and then fetched 21 DE Reg. 722's own Final Order text directly, which confirms Delaware's Division of Social Services struck the drug-felony restriction from Cash Assistance and General Assistance entirely, effective March 11, 2018, implementing House Bill No. 11 (2017) and 31 Del. C. §524. Critically for SNAP specifically: this pack also checked DSSM 9042.2, the Food Supplement Program's own categorical-eligibility household-exclusion list, and confirms it contains NO drug-felony exclusion category at all (it lists ineligible aliens, student-provision ineligibility, fleeing-felon/probation-violator status, institutionalization, and work-requirement noncompliance — but no drug-conviction category). This pack's reading: Delaware has FULLY opted out of the federal drug-felony SNAP ban, not merely modified it, and the secondary sources describing a conditional/modified ban are working from stale information that predates the 2018 repeal. This pack found one internal Delaware manual inconsistency worth flagging precisely: DSSM 9013.2 (Household Concept, in the SEPARATE 9000-series SNAP manual) still lists 'Individuals who are ineligible because of a drug-related felony conviction per DSSM 2027' as one of eleven ineligible-individual categories — a stale cross-reference to a citation that no longer establishes any such ineligibility, since 2027 itself was repealed in 2018. This pack treats the repeal order and DSSM 9042.2's own current exclusion list as authoritative over DSSM 9013.2's stale, uncorrected cross-reference, and flags the inconsistency explicitly in freshness.json rather than resolving it silently.

supplements.citation: DSSM 9060 (Determining Income Deductions); USDA FNS FY2026 Simplified Process for SUA Values memo (08/15/2025)
supplements.heading: DISCLOSED GAP: Delaware's DSSM does not hardcode its own utility-allowance or standard-deduction dollar figures — it defers to a separate, annually-updated 'October Cost-of-Living Adjustment Administrative Notice' this pack could not independently locate for FFY2026
supplements.text: DSSM 9060 confirms Delaware SNAP applies the standard federal deduction structure — a Standard Deduction (amount set by FNS's own October Cost-of-Living Adjustment notice, not hardcoded in DSSM), a 20% Earned Income Deduction, an Excess Medical Deduction for elderly/disabled households with unreimbursed medical expenses over $35/month, a Dependent Care Deduction (actual cost), a Homeless Shelter Deduction, an Excess Shelter Deduction (costs exceeding 50% of countable income, uncapped for households with an elderly/disabled member), and utility allowances split into a Heating/Cooling Standard Utility Allowance (HCSUA, for households with separate heating/cooling costs or LIHEAP payments over $20 in the current or preceding 12 months), a Limited Utility Allowance (LUA, two non-heat/non-cooling utilities), a one-utility standard (one non-heat/non-cooling/non-telephone utility), and a telephone-only allowance — DSSM 9060's own text explicitly says to 'Refer to the current October Cost-of-Living Adjustment Administrative Notice for the standard utility and phone allowance amounts' rather than stating dollar figures itself. This pack tried directly to locate Delaware's own FFY2026 (October 2025) COLA notice PDF and could not find it at a working URL; a 2022-vintage notice URL pattern this pack found (dhss.delaware.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/dss/pdf/OCT2022COLA.pdf) now 404s. USDA FNS's own FY2026 SUA guidance memo (fetched successfully via a reader proxy after a direct 403) confirms that, following the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's prohibition on treating internet costs as a shelter expense, FNS is asking each state to self-calculate its FY2026 SUA values by applying a 2.7% CPI-U adjustment to its own FY2025 baseline rather than publishing one uniform 48-state figure — meaning Delaware's specific current dollar amount is genuinely state-specific and this pack did not locate it. DSSM 9060's own hardcoded figures that this pack DID confirm directly are: a $143.00 Homeless Shelter Deduction and a $35.00 Excess Medical Deduction threshold — but DSSM 9060's amendment footer shows no revision newer than 09/01/14 for the homeless-shelter-deduction subsection, while USDA's current national FY2026 maximum homeless shelter deduction is $198.99; this pack flags that a state MAY legitimately set its own homeless-shelter-deduction figure below the federal cap, so $143.00 is not necessarily wrong, but this pack could not confirm whether Delaware has since raised it and did not find a newer figure to replace it with — see freshness.json.

supplements.citation: Delaware DHSS SNAP Alert page (current, post-11/1/2025 OBBBA exemption list); USDA FNS Delaware FY2025 ABAWD Waiver Response (approved 09/19/2024, expired 9/30/2025); USDA FNS ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY2025-2029 index (no FY2026 Delaware entry)
supplements.heading: Delaware currently has NO active area-wide ABAWD waiver anywhere in the state — the prior Wilmington/Kent/Sussex waiver expired 9/30/2025 and was not renewed, though the federal government-shutdown-driven November 2025 nationwide ABAWD pause temporarily suspended enforcement statewide
supplements.text: An able-bodied adult without dependents (ABAWD) is limited to three countable months of SNAP within a 36-month (3-year) period absent 80 hours/month of a qualifying work activity or an exemption. This pack fetched Delaware DHSS's own live SNAP Alert page directly and confirms the current, post-11/1/2025 OBBBA exemption list: under age 18, age 65 or older (the federal ABAWD age-SCOPE ceiling itself moved from 54 to 64 on 11/1/2025 per this same page), physically/mentally unable to work, pregnant, an 'Indian,' 'Urban Indian,' or 'California Indian' per the Indian Health Care Improvement Act (a newly added exemption), living with someone under age 14 (narrowed from under 18), caring for a child under 6 or an incapacitated person, already working 30+ hours/week or earning $217.50+/week, receiving or having applied for unemployment benefits, attending school/training at least half time, meeting TANF work rules, or participating in a drug/alcohol addiction treatment program. This pack flags explicitly that DSSM 9018.2/9018.3's own regulatory text (last amended 2013) still states the PRE-OBBBA age exemptions (under 18, age 50 or older) — a household or caseworker consulting DSSM directly rather than the live SNAP Alert page would read an outdated age threshold. This pack also found and cross-checked a genuinely time-sensitive, narrow finding: Delaware's own SNAP Alert page states plainly that 'USDA-FNS waived the Able-Bodied Adults Without Dependents (ABAWD) work requirement for November 2025 due to the federal government shutdown and uncertainty around November benefits' — a one-month, nationwide, shutdown-driven pause distinct from Delaware's own area-specific unemployment waiver track. On that separate area-specific track: USDA FNS's own ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY2025-2029 index lists Delaware's most recent posted waiver-response entry as 'FY 2025 Waiver - FNA Response,' approved 09/19/2024 for the combined area of Wilmington city plus Kent and Sussex Counties (based on Bureau of Labor Statistics unemployment data averaging 5.8% for Wilmington and 4.3% for the combined Kent/Sussex area over the 24-month period ending January 2024), effective October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025 — with NO FY2026 entry as of this pack's fetch. This pack's reading: absent a newer request this pack could not find evidence of, Delaware's area-specific ABAWD waiver has lapsed, and the November 2025 shutdown-driven pause was a separate, one-month, already-expired nationwide event, not an ongoing Delaware-specific waiver.

supplements.citation: Delaware DHSS SNAP consumer page (explicit purchase-restriction list); WebSearch corroboration (secondary)
supplements.heading: Delaware does NOT operate a Restaurant Meals Program
supplements.text: The Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) is a state OPTION under 7 CFR § 274.7(g) letting elderly (60+), disabled, and homeless SNAP recipients buy prepared, hot meals from authorized restaurants with EBT year-round. This pack found consistent corroboration across DHHS's own consumer materials (which list 'Hot or prepared foods' explicitly under items you CANNOT buy with SNAP benefits) and secondary-source summaries that Delaware does NOT currently operate an RMP. This pack found no pending Delaware legislation that would establish one. Delaware's operative answer for an applicant asking whether they can use SNAP at a restaurant is a plain no — EBT purchases are limited to grocery-style items for home preparation, with the standard federal exception that SNAP Online Purchasing is available through several Delaware-approved online retailers, a grocery-delivery channel, not a restaurant-meals program.

supplements.citation: DSSM 9068 (Certification Periods) — 12 months standard, 24 months for all-elderly/disabled no-earned-income households
supplements.heading: Delaware's standard SNAP certification period is 12 months, matching the national norm, with 24 months reserved for all-elderly/disabled no-earned-income households
supplements.text: DSSM 9068 states plainly that certification periods 'shall not exceed 12 months' for most households, with DSSM 9068.1 assigning simplified-reporting households a standard 12-month certification period (requiring an interim report in the 6th month) and DSSM 9068.2 assigning a 24-month certification period specifically to households where all members are elderly or disabled and have no earned income (requiring an interim report in the 12th month). This pack flags Delaware's structure as consistent with the 12-month norm most of this roster's other states use, in contrast to this roster's New Hampshire pack, which found a genuinely shorter 6-month standard period. DSSM 9068.3 requires DSS to assign each household the longest certification period possible given its circumstances, with a 4-month floor for households with unstable circumstances, and DSSM 9068.4/9068.5 prohibit shortening a certification period except for confirmed ineligibility or failure to resolve unclear information, while permitting lengthening (up to the 12-month cap for non-elderly/disabled households) when needed.
